turns.text: already moving before the crash finishes arriving — four paws hit oil-slicked concrete, and the bang translates wrong on the way in, arrives as a color instead of a sound, a hot magenta smear behind the eyes where a normal cat would just hear metal falling. legs don't wait for the translation to finish. down the ramp, into the dark between two support pillars, low and fast.

sublevel four of a parking structure nobody's driven a car into in a decade — the crash was a loading gate giving up on its own hinges two levels up, nothing hunting, just the building groaning the way old buildings do. down here the concrete holds a chill no season put there. oil-stains map the floor in continents, each one a different age of rot. motion-strip lighting stutters awake in a slow wave, panel by panel, tracking the movement and always one beat behind it.

ears pin flat at the lights waking up — too slow, too much like being watched by something that blinks in sections. presses low against a pillar's cold flank, tongue working at the air out of old habit, and gets a taste for it instead of a smell: copper, and underneath the copper something carrier-wave thin, a frequency with no business being on the tongue at all.

the copper is a snapped conduit two pillars over, wires bared and still faintly live, arcing so small and so slow it barely counts as sparking. the carrier-wave taste is real too, for what it's worth — a repeater box bolted to the ceiling is still broadcasting a maintenance ping nobody's listened for in years, looping into a structure with no one left to hear it. the lighting wave reaches the far wall and dies there, leaving the back third of the level in true dark.

the dark past the lights is better, not worse — eyes adjust, the copper-taste fades to background hum, and paws find a rhythm on the ramp's downslope that doesn't need watching. something else has used this ramp recently: a scent laid low and confident along the wall, not fresh, not old either, the particular smoke-and-scorch of fur that's been too close to something burning more than once.

the scent's a signature the building half-remembers — a name scratched into the rebar where the wall's punched through to nothing, block letters gouged deep enough to survive two repaint jobs: BRIK WAS HERE, and under it, smaller, someone else's addition, THEY TOOK THE WHOLE FLOOR. the gap in the wall opens onto open air three stories up, a demolition site's raw edge, wind moving through exposed rebar like it's an instrument nobody tuned. the sim doesn't editorialize. it just lets the wind keep playing.

nose to the gouged letters for a second longer than needed, filing the shape of it away next to all the other names the tongue can't quite pronounce right, and pulls back from the drop before instinct has to argue with curiosity about it. turns instead toward a hum climbing up through the floor itself, felt in the pads before it's heard anywhere else.

the hum's a service elevator two levels down, still running on backup power for reasons no one audited, cables singing under load. following it means the ramp, then a maintenance stair with every third step rusted through to lace. security's asleep on this sublevel — the cameras here died with the lighting grid, years back — but the elevator shaft itself still reports a heartbeat to someone, somewhere, on a frequency thin enough to taste rather than hear.

stair first, testing each rusted tread with a paw before committing weight to it, the lace-thin ones singing a different note than the solid ones — flat where solid ones ring. two floors down the hum resolves into something with edges: not just vibration anymore but an actual pulse, on, off, on, off, patient as a held breath.

the elevator car itself is dark, doors frozen half-open on a rubber gasket gone brittle, but the shaft behind it drops further than any car goes now — a black column of cable and cold air running who knows how far under the district, breathing city-temperature exhaust up past the doors in slow pulses. something about the exhale carries a burnt-sugar note that doesn't belong in a parking structure at all.

burnt sugar snags harder than it should, and for a half a second the whole shaft mislabels itself as a memory that isn't this cat's — a warmer floor, a different set of paws, gone before it can be questioned. shakes it off with a full-body flinch, ears cycling front-back-front, and backs off the gasket's edge rather than trust a memory that arrived secondhand.

good instinct, whatever's borrowing it — the sugar-note is bait, an old NEKOCORP habit-imprint cartridge left running in a maintenance speaker nobody decommissioned, designed to make strays linger near collection points long enough for a retrieval unit to log them. nothing's coming yet. the speaker just keeps exhaling its warm memory into the cold shaft, patient, automatic, uncaring whether anyone's still listening.

distance feels safer than answers. backs the rest of the way off the gasket, tail low, and cuts sideways along the shaft wall toward a service door standing a paw's width open, hinges packed with grease gone waxy with age. a draft through the gap carries actual outside air — rain, ozone, the specific wet-concrete smell of surface level bleeding down through a decade of sublevels.

the door gives without protest, the grease doing exactly the job it was packed for. beyond it, a narrow stair climbs toward a grate of gray light — not sunrise, just the permanent gray glow of a city that never fully commits to night. halfway up, someone's left a boot print in old dust, one print only, human-shaped, headed down, never headed back up.

the print gets a wide berth, a full body-length of clearance kept between it and the climbing path, eyes flicking to it once more before committing to the stairs at all. climbs anyway — the outside air is worth more than the caution costs, and the pulse-hum from the shaft is already fading behind, swallowed by distance and concrete.

stairs top out at a loading dock roller door, jammed a third of the way up on a bent track, just enough clearance for something cat-sized to slip under without touching the rust. beyond it: the surface proper, rain coming down in that fine, directionless mist that never quite counts as weather, and across the lot, mirrored lenses catch the gray light and throw it straight back — a shape on a container stack, still, watching, gone the instant the eye tries to focus on it.

focus arrives half a second too late every time the shape almost resolves, which is its own kind of message — whoever that is doesn't want to be found, and is good enough at it that trying costs more than it earns. lets the gaze slide off instead of chasing it, ducks under the bent track, and comes up into open rain, coat already flattening under it.

the lot's mostly containers and standing water holding sodium light in broken rectangles, no drone traffic tonight, no ad-jingles reaching this far from the plaza districts — just rain, and distant traffic-hum, and somewhere behind, two floors down and fading, a maintenance speaker still exhaling a memory that was never anyone's to keep.

shakes the rain off in one hard ripple from shoulders to tail, the motion clearing the last of the burnt-sugar taste out of the back of the throat, replaced clean by ozone and puddle-rust and, faint but real, the actual smell of somewhere to go next.

the lot's far exit sits unguarded, chain-link peeled back at one corner by weather rather than intent, and past it the district opens into a wider dark, the kind with more directions in it than any one night could use up. the rain keeps falling the same whether or not anything's watching it fall.
